catalog_quote: 0. There is one phoneme of stress in Wishram Chinook, as apparently in all other Chinookan dialects.[1] Minimal pairs contrasting in the placement of stress have not been found for three major word-classes, Nouns, Verbs, and Pronouns. ... The occurrence of stress, however, is greatly restricted in terms of a number of recurring patterns. Thus, while no one general rule can be given, the patterns that occur seem to involve but three kinds of factors; these are sentence rhythm, rhetorical uses of stress, and the effect of certain morphemic elements. [fn. 1: ... Comparative references to other dialects supplied by Hymes ...; from Hymes' manuscript grammar of Kathlamet; and from Boas' sketch of Lower Chinook, Shoalwater dialect ...] [sec. 1, p. 238] Typically a word has one and only one phonemic stress, but predictable secondary stress occurs on alternate syllables preceding and following that syllable with primary, phonemic stress. [p. 240] It must be noted that introduction of "inorganic schwa" to bear the accent, so common in Shoalwater Chinook and Kathlamet, is not characteristic of Wishram. ... the alternant k- of the 1st sg. cannot be accented in Wishram (while Shoalwater and Kathlamet dialects accent it by introducing schwa) ... [p. 241] ... these are not mechanically operative rules, such that the placement of stress can be predicted in terms of them. Rather, their interaction results in a complex, partly unpredictable occurrence of stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is a single contrastive (phonemic) word accent whose position is not fixed by a positional rule; the authors (Hymes drawing on his own Kathlamet grammar) extend this 'apparently' to all Chinookan dialects including Kathlamet. In the Wishram analysis placement is largely governed by morphology (polysyllabic stems normally stressed on their first syllable; certain prefixes attract stress; suffixes such as future a-..-ya, distributive -max, -x, -lal etc. draw stress toward the end) and can be overridden by sentence rhythm and rhetorical accent. Kathlamet (like Shoalwater Lower Chinook, unlike Wishram) additionally inserts an accent-bearing epenthetic schwa, e.g. on the 1sg possessive prefix; Boas 1911 independently reports the same E-insertion under accent for Kathlamet and morphological accent shifts (plural -uks to the penult, -ma/-max and future -a toward the word end) for Chinook generally.
new_statements.secondary_stress: For Wishram: 'Typically a word has one and only one phonemic stress, but predictable secondary stress occurs on alternate syllables preceding and following that syllable with primary, phonemic stress' (p. 238); the authors read Boas's late marking of a'qa in Kathlamet Texts as detection of this secondary stress (p. 239). Nothing further specific to Kathlamet.
new_statements.exceptions: Wishram particle minimal pairs (ba'ma vs bama', k'wa'lalak vs k'walala'k, with Kathlamet cognate k'uala'lak Kt 224.3); some monosyllabic verb stems always stressed; plural -ks/-yuks shifts stress only sometimes; future accent shift 'not as regular' in Wishram as in Shoalwater Chinook. Boas 1911 lists Chinook nouns whose accent does not shift in the plural (body-part and kin terms).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic stress explicitly distinguished from sentence rhythm and rhetorical (phrase-final, lengthened) accent; in two-word phrases the first word takes stronger stress. The Kathlamet coverage is a comparative aside in an article on Wishram (wasc1240), supplied by Hymes from his unpublished 1955 Kathlamet grammar; Kathlamet data otherwise rest on Boas's 1890s text transcriptions from one speaker (Charles Cultee).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted article describes Wishram (Wasco-Wishram, Glottolog wasc1240 under Upper Chinook wasc1239); its coverage of Kathlamet (kath1253) is (a) the hedged family-wide claim 'one phoneme of stress.. as apparently in all other Chinookan dialects', explicitly informed by co-author Hymes's own manuscript grammar of Kathlamet (fn. 1), and (b) two specific Kathlamet facts (accent-bearing epenthetic schwa; accented 1sg possessive k- via schwa), which Boas 1911 (Lower/Shoalwater Chinook sketch, chin1286) independently confirms for Kathlamet. All Kathlamet data ultimately derive from Boas's 1890-1894 dictations by a single speaker, Charles Cultee, who also supplied Boas's Lower Chinook texts. Sapir 1909 regards Clackamas (clac1236) as 'very close to Kathlamet, if not identical'.

tone.summary: No tone system described or implied: prosody stated purely as stress - primary stress normally on the penult, first-syllable stress on short unmarked words, secondary stresses on alternate vowels; vowel length and schwa non-phonemic. Nothing on pitch, tone or downstep.
